en: Now begins the chapter on the pacification of rites for those born during eclipses, Chapter 91.
O twice-born one, for those whose birth occurs at the time of a solar or lunar eclipse, there shall be disease, suffering, poverty, and the fear of death. (1)

Therefore, out of a desire for the welfare of people, I shall proclaim the rite of pacification (śānti) regarding the planetary eclipse of the Sun or the Moon that occurs under whichever lunar mansion (nakṣatra). || 2 ||
One should fashion that form of the Lord of the Constellation out of gold;
during a solar eclipse, one should fashion the form of the Sun out of gold according to one's own capacity.
During a lunar eclipse, the wise man should fashion the form of the moon from silver, and likewise the form of Rāhu from lead.
In a clean place, one should smear a level spot with cow dung;
there, one should place a new and very beautiful cloth. || 5 ||
One should have the installation of exactly three forms performed there;
during a solar eclipse, that which is pleasing to the Sun should be offered.
Red unhusked rice, red perfumes, red garlands, garments, and so forth—
whatever is pleasing to the Moon— should be offered during a lunar eclipse.
White fragrance, white flowers, and white garlands, garments, and so forth should be offered to Rāhu; likewise, black flowers, garments, and so forth [should be offered].
Likewise, one should offer white perfumes and other such items to the Lord of the Stars (the Moon);
the wise person should worship the Sun with the mantra beginning with "Ākṛṣṇena."
Then, one should worship the Moon with devotion using the mantra "ime devāḥ," and Rāhu with the mantra "kayā naḥ. || 10 ||

O best of the twice-born, one should offer oblations in sequence with the wood of the *arka*, *pālāśa*, and *samidh* for the Sun and the Moon, and likewise with *dūrvā* grass for the propitiation of Rāhu.
Furthermore, one should offer oblations for the sake of prosperity with fuel-sticks of the *brahmavṛkṣa* tree;
thereafter, one should perform the consecration of the newborn with water from a "quarrel-bath" (*kalahodaka*).
One who is well-composed and has conquered the senses should worship the teacher with devotion;
having fed the Brahmins according to one's ability, one should then dismiss them. 13.
Thus, having performed the pacification rite according to the prescribed rules for one born under the influence of a planet,
and having overcome all obstacles, a man attains good fortune.
Now begins the chapter on the pacification of those born during the junctions of the lunar mansions (gaṇḍānta). || 92 ||
The *gaṇḍānta* of the lunar day (*tithi*), the asterism (*nakṣatra*), and the ascendant (*lagna*) is traditionally held to be of three kinds;
in birth, journeys, marriages, and other such occasions, it brings about death. (1)
O Maitreya, the four nāḍīs at the junction of the lunar days named Pūrṇā and Ānandā, both below and above, are called the *tithi-gaṇḍānta*.
At the junctions of Revatī and Aśvinī, of Pūrva-phalgunī and Maghā, and of Jyeṣṭhā and Mūla, there is likewise a Gaṇḍānta of the constellations consisting of four nāḍīs. || 3 ||
In the junctions between Pisces and Aries, Cancer and Leo, and Virgo and Sagittarius, when these are the ascendants, there is a Lagna-gaṇḍānta measuring one ghaṭī above and below. || 4 ||
Among these, that which is called "unconsumed root" (abhuktamūla) is known as a state of great obstacle;
it lasts for five and eight ghaṭikās respectively at the junctions of Indra and Rākṣasa.
Now I shall describe the rite for pacification for an infant born during a *gaṇḍānta* period;
on the final day of the birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) for one born at such a time, the father [should perform it]. (6)

One should perform the rite of pacification on an auspicious day; until then, one should not look upon that infant, nor upon a bull, at the junction of the *tithi*-groups, nor under the asterism of Dhanu.
One should give gold at the edge of the cheek where it is attached for the pacification of that defect;
furthermore, for one born during the first portion [of the lunar mansion], there should be an ablution for the father as well.

In the second [rite], however, one should cause the consecration of the child and the mother to be performed with gold, or half of that, or according to one's wealth, O best of the twice-born; having fashioned [an image] in the form of the lunar day, the asterism, and so forth, it should be provided with a garment.
One should worship over the site of the quarrel with ritual offerings according to one's ability;
at the conclusion of the worship, one should perform a fire sacrifice (homa) with sacrificial wood, food, and clarified butter according to the prescribed rules.
One should feed Brahmins afterwards; in this way, one is liberated from the fault.
Day by day, one attains long life, health, and prosperity.
Now begins the chapter on the pacification of the Abhuktamūla [constellation], Chapter 93.
Since Indra and the Rākṣasa are the presiding deities of Jyeṣṭhā and Mūla respectively, their conjunction is traditionally held to bestow great evil due to their intense enmity. || 1 ||
One should abandon a son or even a daughter born under Abhuktamūla;
or else, for eight years, the father should not look upon their face.
Now, for the purpose of avoiding those defects, I shall describe the rite of pacification (śānti).
Among these, first the root-pacification (mūla-śānti) is taught because of the abundance of defects.

One should perform the rite of pacification according to the prescribed rules on the twelfth day from birth, or under the same lunar mansion (nakṣatra), or on an auspicious day, or in the eighth year of the child's life.
In a level and auspicious place, smeared with cow dung,
one should construct a pavilion to the east or north of one's own house.

One should construct outside that [mandala] a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) provided with four gates and adorned with archways and other ornaments, for the purpose of sacrifices to the planets and other deities.
One should fashion the form of the deity of the lunar mansion using gold, or half of that, or even half of that again, according to one's available wealth.
He is dark-complexioned, extremely fierce, two-headed, and has the face of a wolf; likewise, he should be meditated upon as holding a sword and a shield, and having a corpse for his vehicle.
Or, having established the value of gold, one should perform worship;
for it is determined in the scriptures that gold belongs to all the deities.
Thereafter, one should choose an ācārya following the ritual recitation of auspicious verses (svastivācana);
then, one should perform the installation of the water-pot (kalaśa) according to the procedure prescribed in one's own Gṛhya-sūtra.
The five products of the cow and so forth, as well as water from sacred fords, should be poured into the jar;
one should also place the hundred medicinal herbs and other ingredients therein within the jar with its hundred holes.
Having placed a bamboo vessel there facing westward,
one should worship the god Nirṛti with white garments, unbroken grains (akṣata), and other offerings.

One should worship Indra as the presiding deity (adhideva) and water as the subordinate deity (pratyadhidaivata), along with the primary deities and others, using the mantras prescribed in their respective Vedic branches.

For the sake of pleasing the God of gods, one who has restrained the senses should perform a fire sacrifice according to the prescribed rules, either one thousand and eight times or one hundred times.
For the purpose of pacifying death, one should recite the Trayambaka mantra;
thereafter, one should respectfully pray to the God for the sake of consecration.
The preceptor, skilled in mantras, should joyfully perform the consecration for the patron who is seated upon an auspicious throne together with his wife and sons.
Immediately after that, one should bathe [the image] with two jars covered by cloths;
likewise, [the officiant] should wear white garments and be anointed with white perfumes. (17)
One should give a milch cow to the preceptor according to one's ability,
provide sacrificial fees to the officiating priests, and also feed the Brāhmaṇas.
Whatever sin and whatever physical ailment resides within all my limbs, consume it all, O Ghee; increase my prosperity and nourishment. (19)
With this very mantra, one should properly examine the clarified butter;
thus, any fault arising from the root or the stalk, as well as the sin of [killing] a serpent, is destroyed.
Now begins Chapter 94: On the Pacification of the *Gaṇḍa* Periods Beginning with Jyeṣṭhā.
One born during the Gaṇḍānta of Jyeṣṭhā brings about the destruction of both his father and himself;
I shall describe the rite for its pacification for the sake of quelling all obstacles. (1)
Everything, including the pavilion and so forth, should be equal in measure to the Mūlaśānti;
Indra is the presiding deity here, and likewise, Fire is the presiding deity there.
And likewise, O Brahmin, one should understand that there is a Rākṣasa presiding over each deity;
one should fashion the form of Indra out of gold according to one's ability.
One should worship the divine deity holding a vajra-hook, seated upon the king of elephants, atop a jar filled with śāli rice.

One should perform the consecration and the fire-oblation (homa) with perfumes, flowers, unbroken grains, and other offerings using the mantras prescribed in one's own Gṛhya-sūtra, and then provide a feast for the Brāhmaṇas.
One should recite the Indra-sūkta with devotion, as well as the Mṛtyuñjaya mantra;
one should also pray to the god Indra, and thereby obtain peace. (6)
Alternatively, in the absence of such capacity, one should indeed perform the gift of a cow;
for the gift of a cow surpasses all other gifts of land.
One should give three cows to a twice-born man born under Mūla, Indra (Jyeṣṭhā), or Maghā; a pair of cows to one born under Revatī or Āśleṣā; and [a single cow] at the junction of the Gaṇḍas.
In the event of any other obstacle or unfavorable conjunction, one should indeed cause a single cow to be given;
and in the absence of a cow, one should give its price to a Brahmin.
A girl born under the Jyeṣṭhā nakṣatra destroys her husband’s elder brother;
a girl born in the final quarter of Viśākhā is a slayer of her husband’s younger brother.
Therefore, at the time of giving her away in marriage, one should also perform the *godāna* ceremony;
[the auspicious times are] those arising from the last three quarters of Āśleṣā and the first three quarters of Mūla.
A daughter and a son are killed respectively by their mother-in-law and father-in-law;
therefore, at the time of their marriage, a wise person should perform a propitiatory rite (śānti).
For the destruction of those defects, one should act according to the extent of one's wealth;
however, in the absence of *dhava*, *agaru*, and *dyu* [wood], no fault arises. || 13 ||
Now begins the ninety-fifth chapter: The Chapter on the Pacification of the Third Rebirth.
Now, O twice-born one, I shall further explain another matter that brings about the defect of birth:
if there is the birth of a daughter in a triad of [lunar] days, and the birth of a son in the subsequent triad; || 1 ||
Then, danger from an ill omen (ariṣṭa) should be known to exist within both the father's and mother's families;
one should perform the rite for pacification there, free from stinginess regarding wealth. || 2 ||
Then, at the end of the period of impurity, or when purified, on an auspicious day and at a favorable time,
having chosen an Ācārya and officiating priests, preceded by a sacrifice to the planets (grahayajña).
One should worship with devotion the auspicious golden images of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśa, and Indra, placed upon a water-pot situated atop a heap of grain. || 4 ||
A single Brahmin, pure and self-controlled, should recite all four Rudra-hymns and all the Peace-hymns at the time of the fire-oblation.
There, the preceptor should offer oblations of sacrificial fuel, clarified butter, sesame seeds, and cooked rice—
either one thousand and eight, or one hundred, or twenty-eight.
Having offered oblations to all the gods beginning with Brahmā using the mantras prescribed in their respective Gṛhya-sūtras,
and then having performed the Sviṣṭakṛt offering, he should again offer the Bali and the Pūrṇāhuti.
One should perform the consecration ceremony for the newborn together with his family;
one should give sacrificial fees to the officiating priests and also feed the Brahmins.
Having performed the inspection of the bell-metal vessel filled with clarified butter, one should satisfy the poor and the helpless;
in this way, O Maitreya, through such pacification, all misfortune is dissolved.
Now begins the ninety-sixth chapter: On the Pacification of the Disturbances of Childbirth.
Now I shall fully explain the transformations arising from procreation, by which there occurs misfortune for the entire village and the family. || 1 ||
If birth occurs at a time that is too early or too late, or if the offspring is deficient in limbs, has redundant limbs, lacks a head, or possesses two heads; || 2 ||
Whether a woman has the form of an animal, or even among animals one has the form of a human—this is a mutation of procreation that arises for the sake of destruction. (3)
If there are abnormalities in a woman or in livestock, or if birth occurs in an unfavorable manner, a great misfortune shall befall that person's family as well. (4)
To avoid those faults, a propitiatory rite (śānti) should be performed with great effort;
or else, one who seeks his own welfare should abandon either a woman or a cow that has calved for the first time.
For a woman, whether it be conception or delivery occurring in the fifteenth year from birth, or even in the sixteenth, it does not result in auspiciousness. || 6 ||
If the Sun is situated in the sign of Leo and Venus is in Scorpio,
the buffalo gives birth and kills its owner, while it itself also perishes.
One should give that [gift] to a Brāhmaṇa or perform a rite of pacification (śānti);
furthermore, there should be worship of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśa, and the planets.
One should perform all rites, such as the fire-oblation (homa) and others, according to the procedure for the three-fold pacification (tritaraśānti).
Thereafter, having become happy at home, one is liberated from all sins.
Thus, when such a misfortune has arrived, the man who performs a rite of pacification attains all his desires; he shall be long-lived and happy. (10)
Now begins the Chapter on the Conclusion (Upasaṃhārādhyāya), 97.
That very weapon which was proclaimed by Brahmā to the high-souled Nārada, that same one Nārada spoke with reverence to Śaunaka and the others. || 1 ||
Therefore, O twice-born one, I have told you this exactly as it was known to me;
it must not be given to one who is envious or to one who delights in censuring others.
This should never be given to one who is dull-witted, ill-behaved, or ignorant;
it should be given to a wise person who is devoted and truthful.
To one who is intelligent, disciplined, and of well-known noble lineage, [he taught] this meritorious science of astrology, the foremost and most excellent limb of the Vedas. (4)
He who knows the measure of time and the configuration of the planets and constellations—
he alone thoroughly understands this science of horā, and no other.

One who knows the true essence of the meaning of the science of horā, who speaks the truth and has conquered the senses, declares the auspicious and inauspicious results; his word shall indeed be true.
For those who read this excellent treatise or listen to it with devotion,
their lifespan, strength, wealth, and fame always increase.
Thus has the wonderful science of horoscopy been declared by Parāśara; this new work, composed of various chapters, is for the delight of modern people. (8)
This supreme [work] was given for the welfare of the world to the twice-born Maitreya;
thereafter, it spread across the earth, honored with devotion by the people.
In this work, the subjects are arranged in separate chapters:
the sequence of creation, the incarnations, and the qualities of the planets and the zodiacal signs.

The special ascendant, the planetary divisions (vargas), their analysis, the aspect on the zodiacal signs, misfortune (ariṣṭa), its annihilation, and likewise the analysis arising from the houses (bhāvas). || 11 ||

The chapter on the results of the houses, as well as the results arising from the lord of the house, the determination of unmanifest results, and the calculation of the aspects of the visible planets. (12)
Then follows the chapter on the clear strength (spaṣṭabala), the calculation of desired and adverse results (iṣṭakaṣṭa), the Pada and Upapada, likewise the Argalā, and then the Karakas. || 13 ||
The results of the karakas and their portions, the chapter on the yoga-karakas, the various celestial yogas, the yoga of the Moon, and the yoga of the Sun; || 14 ||
Thereafter, the Rājayoga is proclaimed, which is the yoga associated with royalty; furthermore, there are specific yogas for the acquisition of wealth, as well as yogas that cause poverty. (15)
The chapters on the killers of life-span and planetary divisions, along with the planetary periods (avasthās) accompanied by their results;
the various chapters on the daśās, combined with the chapter on their specific results. (16)
The internal, intermediate, vital, and subtle designations are its divisions;
as well as the eightfold division (aṣṭakavarga) of the Sun and other planets, and the purification of the trines. || 17 ||

Then follows the purification of the single lordship, followed by the determination of the planetary conjunctions (piṇḍa), and then the clear results of the eightfold divisions (aṣṭakavarga). || 18 ||
After that, the calculation of longevity based on the Aṣṭakavarga, and following that, the clear chapter on the results arising from the collective Aṣṭakavarga. || 19 ||
The chapter on the results of planetary rays, as well as the results of the Sudarśana [diagram], the marks of a Great Man (mahāpuruṣa), and the results of the great elements. || 20 ||

Then follows the chapter on the fruits of the three qualities (guṇatrayaphalādhyāya), as well as the knowledge of the birth-time, the ascendant, and so forth for those whose births are unknown, and the characteristics of renunciation (pravrajyā).

For women, there are various fruits of their actions, as well as the results of auspicious marks; and there are planetary configurations arising from curses due to past sins that cause the loss of sons. (22)
The means for obtaining a virtuous son have been set forth together with the exposition of unfavorable planetary positions, constellations, lunar days, and so forth at the time of birth. (23)
The respective methods for pacifying those [obstacles] have been shown in brief;
and the transformations of childbirth have also been described along with their corresponding rites of pacification.
Thus, one hundred subjects are contained herein in this excellent collection of Jātaka tales;
having understood these, may the wise attain fame and prosperity. (25)
The End of India
